new.statement: The score is mainly set by how many epochs it takes to reach mean accuracy >=0.753. Changes that improve sample efficiency (architecture, optimizer, label smoothing, data selection, averaging) cut time far more than anything else, taking it from the 59.3 s ResNet9 baseline to roughly 10 s.

An airbench96-style network without TTA can be the base recipe and clear the bar in about 10 epochs. Settings: frozen patch-whitening, dirac init, BatchNorm-bias lr x64, lookahead, alternating flip, depth 3, widths 128/384/~576, label smoothing 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, batch size 1024. TTA is forbidden by RULES.md.
Without TTA, the airbench96-style recipe (128/384/576, depth 3, LS 0.3) at <=10 epochs reaches mean accuracy >=0.753 on seeds 0-2, with time <=12 s on the A100-SXM4. The baseline is 59.3 s.

The same recipe at the reported 8.5 epochs, without TTA, lands below 0.753 (expected 0.744-0.752). Getting back to >=0.753 takes >=1 extra epoch, consistent with TTA being worth about 0.65 pp or about 1.2 epochs.
Between 8 and 11 epochs, accuracy rises by >=0.4 pp per extra epoch and roughly linearly. So the knee at 0.753 can be found to within 0.5 epochs (about 5% of time) from a 3-4 point epoch sweep.

Using Muon (orthogonalized momentum) for the 4D conv filters and fused Nesterov SGD for biases and the head, at batch size about 2000, cuts the epochs and wall-clock time needed on CIFAR-100. This mirrors airbench94_muon on CIFAR-10.
Muon (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, nesterov) on the conv filters at batch size 2000 with linear decay to zero reaches >=0.753 in >=10% less time than the tuned SGD airbench96-style base at its own knee.
With 100 classes and short training, stronger label smoothing (about 0.3) regularizes better than the CIFAR-10 default of 0.2. This raises accuracy at a fixed epoch count.
At a fixed recipe and epoch count, LS 0.3 gives >=0.3 pp higher mean accuracy than LS 0.2. LS 0.4 is no better than 0.3 (within 0.15 pp or worse).
Training only on the hardest examples, scored by loss under a cheap proxy model, saves enough compute per epoch to outweigh the proxy's overhead even in an approximately 10-epoch regime.
Training on the hardest 50% of each batch (selected by a small proxy model) reaches >=0.753 with >=10% less time than full-batch training at the matched-accuracy knee.
Widening the last block buys accuracy more cheaply than adding epochs. The final 576-channel block adds little compute, while CIFAR-100's 100-way head benefits from more capacity.
Widening the last block from 512 to 576 at a fixed epoch count gives >=0.3 pp accuracy for <=5% more time per epoch. Net effect: lower time at the 0.753 knee than the 512-wide version.

With the recipe and epochs held fixed, per-step GPU efficiency is a major share of what remains of the time. That covers precision, memory format, kernel fusion and optimizer or Python launch overhead. Systems work can cut time by 10-30% with no change in accuracy.

torch.compile (max-autotune) with channels_last and fp16/bf16 autocast (BatchNorm in fp32) raises throughput substantially. Compilation and warmup happen in build() on synthetic data, so they are untimed.
A compiled, channels_last, half-precision training step cuts train time by >=20% against the same recipe run eagerly in fp32/TF32. Mean accuracy changes by no more than 0.2 pp.

Hiverge-style engineering cuts the remaining per-step overhead in a run of a few seconds: a vectorized or fused optimizer update (foreach/fused, or batched Muon), a fully compiled train step, and SiLU instead of GELU.
On top of H2.1, a fused/foreach optimizer plus a single compiled train step (forward, backward and update) reduces time by >=8%, with accuracy within 0.2 pp.

Progressive resizing, i.e. training the early epochs at lower resolution (cropping to about 24 px) and finishing at 32 px, lowers total FLOPs with little loss in final accuracy. Each resolution is compiled in build().

Running the first ~35% of epochs at 24 px and the rest at 32 px reaches >=0.753 with >=8% less time than training at 32 px throughout. The comparison is at the matched knee and may allow added epochs.

Fixed overheads in the timed prepare/train are >10% of a run of about 10 s. These include loading and decoding data on 4 CPUs, host-to-device copies, normalization, whitening fit, CPU augmentation, and compile or autotune that leaks into the timed region. They can be cut without changing the learning recipe, while staying within the rules.

Keep the whole training set on the GPU as a uint8/half tensor, loaded in prepare, and run augmentation (flip, translate/crop, cutout) as vectorized GPU ops. This removes the bottleneck of a 4-CPU dataloader.
With data and augmentation on the GPU, prepare (load, transfer, normalize, whitening fit) takes <=1.0 s, and per-epoch time is not CPU-bound: GPU utilization stays >=90% during train.

Every compile, autotune and warmup happens in build() on synthetic inputs, covering every shape used later (full and final partial train batch, eval batch sizes). That way nothing recompiles inside the timed region, and no real data is touched in build.
After warmup in build, the first epoch's time is within 10% of later epochs, and no recompilation happens during prepare or train. Eval of any batch size B=1..1024 finishes in <5 s.

The variance across seeds and runs, measured against the 0.753 cutoff on 3 seeds, decides how much over-training is needed. Measuring the noise floor and reducing variance (lookahead/EMA) lets a recipe run closer to its knee, below 0.758 without being fragile.
With seeds fixed, repeated runs of the same recipe differ only through nondeterministic kernels and GPU timing jitter. Both are small compared with the effects we want to detect.
Rerunning an identical recipe 2-3 times gives a spread in mean accuracy of <=0.15 pp and a spread in mean time of <=3%. Smaller differences are marked inconclusive (~).
Weight averaging (lookahead or EMA) raises accuracy at low epoch counts and lowers the spread across seeds. This allows fewer epochs at the same safety margin.
Removing lookahead from the airbench96-style base costs >=0.3 pp of mean accuracy at a fixed epoch count, equivalent to about 1 epoch, and raises the per-seed accuracy std.

structured_output.summary: The tree was empty and there are no results yet, so I seeded it with 4 open Lvl1 hypotheses. H1: sample efficiency, i.e. the number of epochs needed. It covers the airbench96-style base without TTA, Muon at batch size about 2000, label smoothing 0.3, proxy-model hard-example selection, and widening the last block. H2: per-step GPU throughput, covering compile, channels_last and half precision done in build, a fused optimizer with a compiled step, and progressive resizing. H3: fixed overheads in the timed region, covering keeping data on the GPU, augmenting on the GPU, and compiling every shape in build. H4: variance and the noise floor against the 3-seed 0.753 cutoff, covering rerun spread and lookahead/EMA. Each Lvl2 has a numeric Lvl3 prediction. Planned order: (1) run the untouched template as E001; (2) test H1.1.1 and H1.1.2 with an epoch sweep (H1.1.3) to find the knee; (3) run repeats for the noise floor (H4.1.1) before claiming any improvement; (4) then apply the systems levers (H2, H3) and Muon (H1.2). Watch the rules: no TTA, and no real data in build.
